Netflix CEO Ted Sarandos is breaking down why he thinks his streamer lost Stranger Things creators The Duffer Bros. and the hit show’s executive producer and director Shawn Levy to rival studios.

Matt and Ross Duffer surprised the industry by announcing they were jumping ship to Paramount last August in a four-year exclusive deal that covered film and TV. They officially made the switch in April.

Then Levy, who is directing the upcoming Star Wars: Starfighter for Lucasfilm, was announced as leaving for Disney’s 20th Television after a decade spent at Netflix. His deal via his 21 Laps Entertainment production company beings next October.
The Hollywood Reporter asked Sarandos about the high-profile defections of three men who were responsible for what’s arguably the streamer’s biggest hit series.

“The Duffers have worked with us for [a] decade and did not want to make more TV shows right now,” Sarandos said. “They really want to make big tentpole theatrical movies. And I said to Matt and Ross, ‘You guys are great at what you do, and I think you should go do that. You’re 40. Don’t wake up when you’re 60 wishing you did that 20 years later.’ And I’m thrilled for them. They’re going to have great success.”

Sarandos pointed out that Netflix still owns the Stranger Things franchise, which could have still some additional content to come. “We — the Stranger Things universe — are going to continue to be a part of [that success] forever,” he added.
As for Levy, Sarandos suggested the director likewise wanted to make major theatrical films — and suggested that Levy will make more Star Wars movies after Starfighter is released next year.

“Shawn also was kind of doing the same thing. And the problem when you have an overall deal with someone who has commitments in other places, you’re in constant conflict for their time. And Shawn is going to be making Star Wars movies for a while. So the fact that his deal is with Disney makes a lot of sense. I’m thrilled for Shawn. We’re going to do a ton of things together.”
Sarandos added Netflix still has shows in development with Levy, including an upcoming hockey drama titled Sticks. “We have a lot of that stuff’s going to stick around,” he said.

The Duffer Brothers have similarly explained that movies were their reason for leaving Netflix, with Matt Duffer saying, “The biggest draw to us was just to be able to do something theatrical, which is not something Netflix does.”
Levy’s statement about his Disney deal was more vague, saying he has “always felt a kindred spirit in Disney and their storytelling ethos” and noting the studio “feels like home.”
Talia Ryder is the latest star lacing up their dance shoes for Tom Holland’s Fred Astaire biopic.

The Sony production about the legendary dancer and actor of Hollywood’s Golden Age has already tapped Margaret Qualley to play Adele Astaire, Fred’s older sister and Broadway partner, and Sabrina Carpenter as Ginger Rogers, Fred Astaire’s frequent film co-star. Ryder, a classically trained dancer, will play June Allyson, a dancer and MGM actress who was originally set to star opposite Astaire in the musical film Royal Wedding.
Paddington filmmaker Paul King is directing from a screenplay he wrote with Steven Levenson based on the book The Astaires: Fred & Adele by Kathleen Riley.

Amy Pascal and Rachel O’Connor produce for Pascal Pictures along with Ben Holden and Josh Hyams for Lightbulb Pictures and Holland for Billy17. Steven Levenson and King penned the script based on the book The Astaires: Fred & Adele by Kathleen Riley.
The film has support from some Astaire family members, including Fred’s daughter, Ava Astaire McKenzie. Her son, Tyler McKenzie, serves as a consultant and co-producer.

Ryder‘s onscreen credits include a breakout in Sundance indie Never Rarely Sometimes Always and Ethan Coen’s Honey Don’t, where she appeared opposite Qualley. As for musical cred, Ryder had a role in Steven Speilberg’s adaptation of West Side Story and began her career in Broadway‘s Matilda the Musical.
Ryder, who is repped by UTA, LBI and Vainshtein Law, will next be seen in Amazon MGM’s 4 Kids Walk Into A Bank and the second season of Amazon Prime’s Mr. & Mrs. Smith.
Bruno Mars may have just found the perfect way to get Karol G back.

Just days after joking that he needed to “get” the Colombian superstar back from Drake, Mars has recruited Karol G for the new music video for his lovely The Romantic track “Dance With Me,” released Thursday (Oct. 1).

The video opens with Mars strumming an electric guitar all by his lonesome, pleading the lyrics into a pay phone. Karol is on the other line, sulking in bed in a lace outfit. Mars moves on from the telephone booth to where Karol resides, serenading her from below her balcony with a full band behind him. It’s a dreamy, old-fashioned serenade, with Mars singing to Karol as the instruments flourish. Karol makes her way below, jumping into Mars’ arms as fireworks explode in the sky. The duo stares into each other’s eyes as the video comes to a close, ending the night on a wholesome — and, quite literally, a romantic — note.
It’s a fitting visual for “Dance With Me,” which finds Mars leaning into the kind of swooning romance that has become a signature theme within his discography.

And Karol G’s appearance comes at a bit of a funny time in their ongoing musical friendship. On Monday (Sept. 28), Mars reacted to a viral video of Drake dancing with Karol G during the rapper’s surprise appearance at her Houston concert. Posting a photo of himself staring dramatically out of the window of a private jet, Mars jokingly wrote, “I have to get her back! I must get her back! I will get her back!”

Mars and Karol G already have some musical history together, as the pair teamed up on “Still,” an all-English-synth-pop ballad from Karol G’s sixth studio album, No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto. The collaboration reached No. 41 on the Billboard Hot 100, while the album debuted at No. 8 on the Billboard 200.
They also took “Still” to the stage together for the first time when Mars surprised fans during Karol G’s Aug. 15 concert at Los Angeles’ SoFi Stadium.

For Mars, “Dance With Me” is the closing track on The Romantic, his first solo album in nearly a decade. The album debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, while “Dance With Me” opened at No. 42 on the Billboard Hot 100.

Pophouse Entertainment said on Thursday (Oct. 1) it acquired a 50% stake of Australian singer-songwriter Sia’s publishing and master music rights, according to a joint statement from the artist and Swedish entertainment company that owns rights to music by KISS, Cyndi Lauper, Iron Maiden and Tina Turner.

“I’m really excited to be working with Pophouse,” the “Elastic Heart” artist said in the statement. “These songs mean so much to me, and I love that they really understand that and want to take care of them. I’ve been making music for a very long time now, and it feels exciting to think about all the new and different ways these songs might get to live on and find people. I’m really looking forward to seeing what we can dream up together.”

Sia and Pophouse declined to disclose terms of the deal, which included her Billboard Hot 100 chart topper “Cheap Thrills,” which features Sean Paul. TMZ reported the artist will receive $165 million for rights to the songs she wrote before 2022, with an additional $15 million for songs written after 2022 that will be held in escrow, according to its story on Tuesday (Sept. 29).

Born Sia Furler, the pop star gained acclaim for her contributions to hits like Rihanna‘s “Diamonds” and Beyoncé‘s “Pretty Hurts.” The pop star’s unmistakable voice rose to international prominence following the release of her 2014 album 1000 Forms of Fear and its Top 10 hit “Chandelier.”

Pophouse acquired Sia’s catalog with its Pophouse Fund I, which it closed with $1.3 billion in 2025 and tapped to fund the acquisition of rights to songs by KISS, Cyndi Lauper, Avicii and Swedish House Mafia.

“Sia is an artist whose extraordinary catalog and unique creative identity offer exceptional opportunities to celebrate and build on her remarkable body of work,” Pophouse CEO Jessica Koravos said in the statement. “This partnership will further empower Sia with strategic support and creative resources to continue pursuing her artistic ambitions while preserving and expanding her influence.”

Sia continues to make music, releasing “Awake Tonight” in April with Afrojack and David Guetta 15 years after the trio’s hit “Titanium.” Another Sia-Guetta collaboration, “Beautiful People” topped Spotify’s Australian Music Global Impact List in February. The chart ranks the most globally streamed songs by Australian artists.

The transaction follows what the artist has publicly called the “difficult year” defined by her bitter divorce with ex-David Bernhad and custody settlement requiring her to pay $42,500 according to month in child support.

Anthony Anderson is set to host the 2026 Soul Train Awards, airing Friday, Nov. 27, at 8 p.m. ET/PT on BET and CBS. This is the first Soul Train Awards since 2023 and the first ever to air on CBS. The two-hour show will tape on Thursday, Nov. 5, at Harris Theater in Chicago.

“I’m thrilled to be back with BET and especially excited to host Soul Train Awards in Chicago, where the Soul Train legacy began,” Anderson said in a statement. “Soul Train is more than a television show or an awards franchise; it’s a piece of our cultural history. Don Cornelius created a platform that gave Black artists a place to shine, and generations later, that spirit is still alive. I’m looking forward to celebrating the legends, the artists shaping R&B and soul today, and bringing a whole lot of fun to the night.”

Anderson, best known for his role on ABC’s long-running Black-ish, previously hosted the Soul Train Awards in 2013. The actor-comedian has an extensive resume as an awards show host. He hosted the NAACP Image Awards for nine consecutive years (2014-22) and the 75th Annual Primetime Emmy Awards in 2024. He cohosted the BET Awards in 2015 and 2016 with his Black-ish costar Tracee Ellis Ross.

“Anthony brings an incredible combination of comedic instinct, musical knowledge and genuine love for this culture,” said Connie Orlando, evp of specials, music programming and music strategy for BET. “His longstanding relationship with BET, coupled with his experience hosting some of television’s biggest award shows, makes him a natural fit for this new chapter of Soul Train Awards.”

“Anthony Anderson is an exceptional entertainer with a genuine connection to BET and the culture that Soul Train represents,” said Louis Carr, president of BET. “He understands the legacy, the music and the importance of creating a moment that brings people together. As we return Soul Train Awards to Chicago, the birthplace of the franchise, we’re excited to have Anthony at the center of this celebration.”

For his work on Black-ish, Anderson received seven consecutive Primetime Emmy nominations for outstanding lead actor in a comedy series (2015-21), four Primetime Emmy nominations for outstanding comedy series as an executive producer, three Golden Globe nominations and three Critics’ Choice nominations. He has won eight Image Awards and received six BET Award nominations.
We all love a win-win. Well here's one better–a potential win-win-win.
By using what would otherwise be an industrial waste in new road pavements, the future of highways and byways could reduce impacts on climate change and potentially save lives.

A new analysis suggests that replacing conventional urban pavement with roads made partly from recycled steel slag could substantially cut greenhouse gas and air-pollution emissions, while also reducing road maintenance (so fewer annoying road-repair traffic jams, too!).
If you've never heard of steel slag, you're not alone. It's actually a waste product that comes out of the process of melting iron ore or scrap metal to make steel.
This leftover stuff is a mix of silicon dioxide and metal oxides and it can be used to make steel slag epoxy asphalt mixture, or SEAM.
Steel slag is kind of ideal for pavement because its high strength and angular structure make it useful for creating a durable road material.
In this study, the researchers combined the SEAM with an epoxy-modified asphalt binder, producing a material designed to withstand wear and deformation better than conventional pavement.
A more durable road reduces the social annoyance and air pollution of road-construction-related congestion.

But also, as pavement deteriorates, vehicles actually use more fuel (costly on its own both financially and in emissions). So if a road deteriorates less often, it also saves the vehicles that ride on it gas, diesel, and wear-and-tear.
In the researchers' model, all these use-phase effects accounted for about 95 percent of emissions and 60 percent of the lifetime costs of the road in the baseline scenarios.

Even though most of the costs for any roadway happen in the use phase, the researchers do show that SEAM costs more to build, produces more emissions and generates more fine particulate pollution during its early years of use. But crucially, just when a conventional roadway surface needs replacement (generating those emissions again), the SEAM-based roadway emissions keep going.
This significant durability of the SEAM-based roadways changes the equation.

The researchers modeled three versions containing 20, 35 or 50 percent epoxy. Conventional pavement and 20 percent epoxy SEAM were assumed to last six years, while the 35-percent epoxy version lasted an estimated 15 years and the 50-percent version 20 years.

By spreading the emissions and costs of construction over a longer service life – and reducing the fuel and maintenance penalties associated with deteriorating roads – the longer-lasting pavement could eventually make up for its higher upfront footprint.

The researchers identified the 35-percent epoxy formulation as the best balance within their modeled scenarios: More epoxy extended pavement life, but beyond roughly 35 percent, the additional environmental gains leveled off while costs continued to rise.

They then scaled the model up to China's urban road network, testing scenarios in which 25, 50, 75 or 100 percent of existing urban asphalt pavement was replaced. At the highest replacement level, the model projected reductions of about 1.74 billion tonnes of CO2-equivalent emissions and 1.23 billion kilograms of PM2.5 over the assessment period.
PM2.5 is the fine particulate pollution that's linked to deaths from heart disease, kidney disease, dementia, hypertension, lung cancer, and other diseases.

Those numbers add up to create a pretty serious impact. Across the replacement scenarios, the researchers estimated 31,802 to 128,980 premature deaths could be avoided as a result of reduced PM2.5 exposure alone.

Those health figures come from a model linking modeled reductions in fine particulate pollution with established relationships between PM2.5 exposure and mortality. The authors explicitly describe the results as system-level estimates rather than precise epidemiological predictions.
Not to be overlooked, SEAM could also save some serious money: It could generate 3.48–15.01 trillion Chinese Yuan ($519.14 billion to $2.24 trillion US Dollars) according to the study.

These kinds of system-level material performance changes could have even larger implications as they're "broadly transferable to other rapidly urbanizing economies with significant steel industries," the study's researchers write.

"Countries such as India, along with several nations in Southeast Asia and Africa, generate large volumes of [steel slag] while facing accelerating transport demand and mounting environmental constraints." Those countries could also benefit from the climate, public health, and economic gains of the SEAM roadways.

There are logistical complications to account for: Steel slag isn't produced evenly across China, so the researchers modeled shipping it between provinces. That adds emissions – but in their model, the additional transport still produced a large net reduction in CO2-equivalent emissions and PM2.5.

The study also doesn't model whether today's industrial infrastructure could immediately produce and distribute enough material to meet nationwide demand. And one of the biggest drawbacks is that this new pavement requires seven days of curing before it can fully open to traffic.

It's interesting to think that a more sustainable roadway may not necessarily be the one that takes the least energy to build. It could be one that spends the longest time being boringly, gloriously roadlike – smooth, durable, and in need of fewer repairs.
The research has been published in Communications Earth & Environment.
The Space Development Agency is set to launch 21 Tranche 1 data transport satellites on Oct. 5—its fourth Tranche 1 mission since last fall and the first to carry Northrop Grumman-built satellites.

The launch is scheduled for 1:15 a.m. local time from Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif., on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. Once in orbit, the 21 spacecraft will join 63 Tranche 1 satellites built by York Space Systems and Lockheed Martin.

The mission represents a few firsts for Northrop. It’s not only the contractor’s inaugural Tranche 1 launch—the company is on the hook for another batch of 21 Tranche 1 Transport satellites and 14 missile tracking spacecraft—but it’s also the firm’s first time delivering and operating such a large quantity of satellites. SDA Director Gurpartap Sandhoo told reporters during an Oct. 1 prelaunch call that based on some of the challenges other providers have had with scaling, he expects there will be some challenges.

“It’s one thing to go through launch and early ops of one, two, maybe even three or four satellites. Twenty-one is a completely different ball of wax,” said Sandhoo, who is also the Space Force’s portfolio acquisition executive for missile warning, tracking, and defense. “We’ll see some issues, but I’m confident the team at Northrop … the issues that pop up, any patches, any updates we have to do, they’re ready to go.”

Since SDA started in 2019 to build out a proliferated constellation of data transport and missile warning satellites in low Earth orbit, the agency has faced setbacks that have delayed launches and fielding timelines. While it had hoped to have all 154 of its Tranche 1 satellites in low-Earth orbit by this summer, supply chain issues and technical challenges on the ground and in orbit disrupted those plans. Sandhoo has attributed many of those slowdowns to the challenges that come with building and launching satellites in large numbers.

“The issue has not been the capability of the system,” Sandhoo told reporters. “The issue has been building them at scale, getting them tested at scale, launching them at scale, doing the launch and early ops at scale. It’s the volume of these things that has been a challenge.”

Following the launch of York and Lockheed’s first spacecraft last year, initial on-orbit checkout and testing took much longer than the four to six months SDA expected. The agency ended up taking a nine-month pause to sort out issues on orbit and make changes on the ground to ensure its next satellites didn’t run into the same hiccups.

In July, SDA resumed Tranche 1 launches, flying York’s last 21 transport satellites. Checkout of those spacecraft went much smoother, Sandhoo said. Since then, the agency has moved control of York’s satellites into its operations center and started doing some limited experimentation. SDA has had some issues transferring Lockheed’s spacecraft to the operations center. To date, it’s only been able to move four, and Sandhoo said the company and SDA are working through the engineering issues to understand the cause and make sure it’s addressed before Lockheed launches more satellites.

“As we get the rest of the architecture, the rest of the planes up, it’s going to get more complicated,” he said. “We need to make sure the understanding is there, the behavior, and the dependability. Being able to get them in the ops and working properly is critical.”
A spokesperson for Lockheed told Air & Space Forces Magazine the company is working closely with SDA to transition the satellites to the agency’s control centers.

“These experiences are an important part of developing new, integrated space systems and we’re focused on ensuring reliability and mission success during this transition, while still moving quickly as a team,” Lockheed said. “We will apply lessons learned from each plane into future efforts.”

While the agency isn’t out of the woods yet in terms of schedule and scaling woes, Sandhoo told reporters he expects that as companies and their suppliers get used to building and flying larger numbers of satellites, their performance will improve. But for now, he said, he’s not satisfied with the time it’s taken to get to this point.

Asked what SDA could have done differently to avoid these setbacks, Sandhoo said it’s possible that for the early tranches of satellites, the agency could have required more insight into the companies’ processes rather than opt for the more hands-off approach it took in its contracting strategy.

“We are trying to get to a place where we can have a capability-driven architecture. We tell them what the system needs to do, and our vendors and our industrial base builds that out to that spec with minimal oversight,” he said. “Maybe we should have, for the first tranche, been probably more intrusive in that process than we were.”

Following the Oct. 5 launch, SDA is eyeing its first Tranche 1 tracking layer mission either in December or early next year. Beyond that flight, it’s hoping to finish the last four launches and have all Tranche 1 satellites in orbit by late spring 2027.
The Navy failed to identify and treat special warfare personnel who exhibited symptoms of a traumatic brain injury, a government watchdog found.

The Defense Department Inspector General published a report Wednesday that criticized Naval Special Warfare Command for relying on an evaluation system that fell prey to a lack of oversight and compliance.

“The Naval Special Warfare Command did not consistently implement Do[D] and Naval Special Warfare Group Four (NSWG-4) policies regarding the identification, clinical evaluation, and subsequent care of SWCCs presenting symptoms of TBI,” the report found.
The Defense Department defines a traumatic brain injury as one that disrupts brain function as a result of external force.
The indications of TBI are identified through changes in mental function, including confusion and slower processing; memory loss; and dips in consciousness.

Navy special warfare personnel are required to fill out a mild TBI and Exposure Report form after returning from being away at sea and report any symptoms they’ve experienced that may be related to TBI.

If that person reports or displays symptoms indicative of a concussion, medical personnel perform an evaluation and screening called a Military Acute Concussion Evaluation, Version 2, to try to diagnose a concussion and a TBI.
But the Defense Department Inspector General found that many service members returning from an underway never filled out the report.

Between Jan. 1 and April 1, 2026, only 24 sailors with Naval Special Warfare Command completed the form, accounting for just 21 of 193 underways reported by Special Boat Team 12 and Special Boat Team 20 during that period.
The inspector general said this happened because there is currently no program that oversees the form-filling process or enforces compliance.
The watchdog found no evidence that commanders and senior leaders made sure service members completed the forms.
The forms also take several hours to complete, which discourages sailors from finishing the important paperwork.
Most importantly, over the span of six years, Naval Special Warfare Command didn’t record a single completed MACE-2 test for Special Boat Team 12 and Special Boat Team 20.

Between 2020 and 2026, 144 service members completed 634 TBI Exposure Forms after exhibiting symptoms of TBI, but not one of them underwent the concussion evaluation MACE-2 test meant to diagnose TBI.
The inspector general said this problem arose because the Navy’s concussion management plan only requires a corpsman to conduct a MACE-2 test if the service believes the sailor has a concussion.
But there is no foolproof way to identify a concussion, the inspector general said, leaving massive room for human error.
Medical personnel don’t conduct a MACE-2 unless the Navy special warfare service member, or senior official above them, asks for it.
Symptoms listed on the mild TBI and Exposure Report form also include maladies that don’t only pertain to concussions, making it unclear what may be indicative of a concussion.
The inspector general discovered that Navy special warfare personnel also sometimes deliberately circumvent the TBI process by providing answers to the MACE-2 test they have memorized beforehand.
These answers are delivered to downplay the severity of any potential symptom or injury.
The government watchdog said the weakness of the test is a byproduct of the Defense Department not having a standardized test for wave-impact events.
Naval Special Warfare Command additionally failed to ensure that service members displaying TBI symptoms arrived for follow-up appointments for medical attention.
The Navy’s concussion management plan requires a service member to return for a medical follow-up appointment within two weeks of returning to duty.
But none of the 634 TBI Exposure Forms completed between 2020 and 2026 documented a completed follow-up appointment within that time frame.
One Navy special warfare service member told the inspector general that fear of losing their job on the boat played into ditching follow-up appointments.
They said reporting symptoms could derail deployment exercises.

In response to their report, the inspector general recommended that Naval Special Warfare Command develop a more comprehensive way to identify TBI in special warfare combat crewmen and ensure service members receive follow-up treatment.

The government watchdog also recommended that Naval Special Warfare Command’s senior medical officer work closely with the branch chief of the Traumatic Brain Injury Center of Excellence to institute a standardized checklist to assess TBI from wave impacts.
Riley Ceder is a Navy reporter at Military Times, where he covers issues directly affecting service members and their families, as well as breaking news.
For ESA astronaut Sophie Adenot, her first steps into space were only the beginning.
In less than 15 days, she performed three extravehicular activities, or EVAs, spending 19 hours and 42 minutes outside the International Space Station.

Across three demanding spacewalks, Sophie and her crewmates replaced critical Station hardware, installed a new communications antenna, carried out maintenance, and prepared experiments for future work, all while adapting to the challenges of working in the extreme environment of space.
From her very first spacewalk to leading her third as EV1, Sophie demonstrated what it takes to work beyond Earth: technical skill, perseverance, adaptability, and trust in the teams supporting you.

A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket took off on a flight to the International Space Station Thursday carrying two NASA astronauts, a cosmonaut and a Canadian whose wife plans a launch of her own later this year, giving birth to the couple’s third child while her husband is away in space.

Strapped into a SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule, Crew 13 commander Jessica Watkins, pilot Luke Delaney, Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov and Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk blasted off from pad 40 at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 11:10 a.m. EDT.
The launch originally was planned for mid September, but the flight was delayed to replace a leaking valve in the Crew Dragon’s propulsion system.

Watkins, who holds a Ph.D. in geology, flew to space aboard a Crew Dragon in 2022. Her crewmates are space rookies, the 296th, 297th and 298th astronauts to fly aboard the ISS. Delaney and Kutryk are both former military test pilots while Teteryatnikov served in the Russian submarine force before becoming a cosmonaut.

Kutryk and his wife Heather have two children, ages 5 and 7. They’re expecting their third child around Thanksgiving, about two months into the Crew 13 mission. In so doing, they will become the fourth couple in space history to have a child born while one parent was off the planet.

“Leaving these three (plus one on the way) is the hardest thing I’ve ever done,” Kutryk wrote in a post on the social media platform X. “But that has always been the nature of exploration.” He then quoted Norwegian arctic explorer Fridtjof Nansen, describing his thoughts upon setting off for the North Pole.

“‘Behind me lay all I held dear in life. And what lay before me? Happy child, little do you know what life is — how strangely mingled and how full of change… and now, a farewell to home. It was the darkest hour of the whole journey.'”

Despite President Trump’s recent animosity toward Canada, the Canadian Space Agency continues to play a major role in the U.S. space program. Along with supplying the robot arms that helped build the space station, CSA astronaut Jeremy Hansen flew around the moon on NASA’s Artemis II mission. Kutryk is the 17th Canadian to fly in space.

“When I think about the space station, I hope the legacy is that people see this beacon in the sky going around Earth, one of the most complex things humans have ever, ever created, and they see it for all of its technical marvel and all the science and discoveries we’re making there,” he said.

“But (I hope) they also see it as sort of this beacon for what we can do when we make good decisions, when we work together and we collaborate and we prioritize things. It’s testament to what we’ve done, what we can do, and really to what we hope the generations that follow can do.”

After boosting the Falcon 9 and Crew Dragon capsule out of the dense lower atmosphere, the Falcon 9’s first stage flew itself back to a pinpoint landing at the Space Force station while the rocket’s upper stage continued the climb to space. Minutes later, the second stage engine shut down and the crew capsule separated to fly on its own.

“What an epic ride!” Delaney radioed. “What an epic ride it was! Today, we proudly continue the streak of humans living and working in orbit, building on the legacies of yesterday to pave the way for future of space exploration … Deepest appreciation to my family and friends who stood by me throughout this entire endeavor. Thank you. I love you guys. And to the Marines back on Earth, Semper Fi.”

Like all flights to the International Space Station, piloted and unpiloted alike, the Crew 13 launch was timed for the moment Earth’s rotation carried the pad into the plane of the station’s orbit. That’s a requirement for rendezvous missions because no current rockets have the power to overcome their orbital momentum and change their direction of travel when moving at nearly 5 miles per second.

While a Falcon 9 cannot change orbital planes, the Crew Dragon capsule can change its altitude as required, flying lower — and faster — to catch up with its quarry and higher to slow down the approach.

In this case, it will take Crew 13 capsule just eight hours — a NASA record — to catch up with the ISS, moving in for an automated docking at the forward port of the station’s Harmony module at 7 p.m.

“I personally am looking forward to returning to the ISS as well as flying on Dragon a second time, and really looking forward to experiencing those experiences through the eyes of my crewmates,” Watkins said.

“We expect a very busy mission with lots of station maintenance, both internal and external, with a few EVAs (spacewalks) on the docket as well as visiting vehicle capture and stowage operations, lots of science … and plenty of outreach.”

Standing by to welcome Watkins and company aboard will be the crew they are replacing: Crew 12 commander Jessica Meir, pilot Jack Hathaway, European Space Agency astronaut Sophie Adenot and cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev. They’re wrapping up a 235-day mission that began with launch atop a Falcon 9 rocket on Feb. 13.
Godspeed Crew-13! pic.twitter.com/W3r5aeAPHg
— Jessica Meir (@Astro_Jessica) October 1, 2026

Also on board: Soyuz MS-29/75S cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina and NASA astronaut Anil Menon, launched on a Soyuz 2.1a rocket from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan on July 14. They’re in the midst of an eight-month stay, returning to Earth in early April 2027.

After an expedited “crew handover,” during which Meir and her crewmates will show their replacements the ins and outs of station operations, Crew 12 will board their own Crew Dragon capsule and return to Earth. Undocking is planned for Oct. 5 with splashdown in the Pacific Ocean off the southern California coast on Oct. 6.

“I think the thing that I’m looking forward to most is seeing my three-and-a-half-year-old daughter,” said Meir, a two-flight veteran with seven spacewalks to her credit. “I’m so looking forward to seeing nature again, feeling the breeze on my face, the wind rustling through the leaves, experiencing all those things that we don’t have up here.
“But I will very, very much miss being weightless all the time and the incredible views that we have.”

Said Hathaway: “Going home and being able to take a nice long hot shower will be very relaxing and very nice. And, of course, I’m looking forward to seeing my family. But a hot shower is near the top of my list.”

Crew 12’s departure will free up the Harmony module’s space-facing port for the arrival of a SpaceX Cargo Dragon on Oct. 13 that will be loaded with crew supplies, science gear, spare parts and two roll-out solar array panels. The Crew 13 fliers also expect to welcome a Northrop Grumman cargo ship in December, along with two Russian Progress freighters in November and February.

The roll-out solar arrays going up on the next Dragon Cargo ship are the final sets in a major upgrade to the station’s original solar power system that began with initial installations in June 2021. The final two sets will be installed during spacewalks late this month and early November.
Dragon separates from Falcon 9’s second stage pic.twitter.com/Ay7VmubfF6

But the major goal of the flight, like all NASA missions to the station, is conducting research in the microgravity environment of space. Scores of experiments and technology demonstrations are running at any given moment with fresh studies going up on virtually every flight.
The Crew 13 fliers will face the same challenges.

“During the mission, the crew will help us fight heart disease and Parkinson’s disease by studying human stem cell-derived tissues that will help improve medicine, disease modeling, and pharmaceutical testing,” said Dana Weigel, director of NASA’s low-Earth orbit mission directorate.

“They will also explore crop production that’s important for longer-duration spaceflight missions, and they’ll help us better understand blood flow abnormalities that we see in space, along with testing new diagnostic medical equipment for monitoring crew health. That’s just a couple of the highlights of the research the crew will be doing on board.”
All in all, Hathaway said, the crew is looking forward to an action-packed stay in space.

“For me, between the science, the spacewalks and everything else that the expedition is going to have, it’s looking to be a great time,” Delaney said. “Excited to launch with this crew, join the expedition, and integrate as an extension of NASA and all the ISS team members. So exciting times ahead!”
On Sept. 22, NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope’s Coronagraph Instrument opened its eyes to cosmic light for the very first time.

Designed and built by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, the coronagraph will demonstrate cutting-edge technology to block starlight and view planets and dusty disks around nearby stars.

The instrument woke up on Sept. 1 and stretched its digital, electronic, and mechanical “limbs” mid-month. Once the team confirmed that the fine-guidance system was holding the Coronagraph Instrument steady, scientists adjusted the focus so it could take its first bleary-eyed look at space that will help scientists fine-tune the instrument’s view.

“This observation confirms that the instrument can produce a focused image,” said Vanessa Bailey, a Roman Coronagraph Instrument scientist at NASA JPL. “It’s a very limited test that kicks off a methodical process of increasingly complex tasks that help us prepare for the instrument’s future observations.”

As part of NASA’s ongoing Inspiration Tour, NASA astronaut Christina Koch will highlight America’s strengths in space exploration and aeronautics innovation at the Philadelphia Eagles vs. Los Angeles Rams game in Philadelphia on Sunday, Oct. 4.

A self-proclaimed Philadelphia sports fan, Koch is an explorer and engineer who spent a total of 338 days in space across two missions, including serving as a mission specialist for the agency’s Artemis II mission earlier this year. On April 1, Koch launched from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida aboard the Orion spacecraft on top of the agency’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket as part of Artemis II. Koch and her fellow crew members completed a historic lunar flyby, marking humanity’s return to the vicinity of the Moon for the first time in more than 50 years.

NASA team members will engage with fans at the agency’s Experience Zone, located outside the stadium from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. before the game. Fans can learn more about NASA’s return to the Moon through the agency’s Artemis program, enjoy interactive games, and capture photos at a selfie station and with a large, inflatable NASA logo.

With stops across the nation, NASA’s Inspiration Tour convenes academic, industry, and public sector stakeholders to connect the agency with the people, technologies, and organizations that drive American leadership in space.

The tour will culminate in MAX POWER, a public exposition of American air and space innovation, Saturday, Nov. 7, and Sunday, Nov. 8, on and near the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Held in honor of America’s historic 250th anniversary, the multi-day, family-friendly event will showcase the next-generation aircraft, spacecraft, autonomous vehicles, and technologies that will help define the future of transportation in air and space.

Saudi Arabia is planning an offensive against Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen, with options being considered, including a coastal push to secure the Red Sea shipping route or an assault on multiple fronts, regional and Western officials told Reuters.

The operation, expected to be launched in the coming weeks, will be led by Yemeni forces on the ground, which are overseen by Riyadh, and supported by Saudi air strikes, according to six people with knowledge of the preparations.

While the US is already providing intelligence to support Riyadh’s operations in Yemen, and some regional and European nations are providing mainly defensive military aid to the kingdom, the Saudi allies aren’t expected to play a direct role in combat operations, said the people who requested anonymity to discuss security matters.

Saudi Arabia entered neighboring Yemen’s civil war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition in support of the internationally recognized government, which the Houthis had driven out of the capital Sanaa. A truce agreed between the warring parties in 2022 largely held until this year, when the Houthis launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi shipping and oil infrastructure in a spillover from the Iran war.

A key objective of the planned Saudi offensive, which hasn’t been previously reported, is aimed at reversing the rapid gains made by the Houthis last month when they advanced down the coast and seized control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait, according to people with knowledge of the plans who include Gulf and Yemeni officials and Western diplomats.

The Saudis are considering two options for the assault, the Gulf and Yemeni officials said: either a narrowly focused attack around Bab el-Mandeb or a broader offensive that also includes synchronized attacks on multiple fronts around Yemen, in the governorates of Al-Bayda, Marib, Taiz and Al-Jawf.
More than 100,000 Yemeni troops could be mobilized in the offensive, depending on the scale, the officials all said.
Spokespeople for the Saudi and Yemeni governments, the Houthi group and the US military didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment about the Saudi plans.

Bab el-Mandeb is the southern exit passage of the Red Sea, a key shipping route between the Mediterranean and Asia that’s assumed even more importance this year as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively closed by the Iran conflict.

Riyadh has concluded it cannot enter new Yemeni peace negotiations with the Houthis while the militants remain in control of Bab el-Mandeb, giving them significant global leverage, the Western diplomats and Gulf official said.

The six people with knowledge of the Saudi preparations couldn’t give a precise timing for the launch of the offensive, with their estimates ranging from within a week to after the US midterm elections in early November.

Michael Ratney, a former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia, said he expected an offensive to be narrowly focused and certainly more modest in scope than the Saudi-led operation in 2015 that sought to rout the militants.

“As much [as] they want to vanquish the Houthis completely, they also need to get back to status quo ante before Houthis controlled territory along Bab el-Mandeb,” he added. “Ideally, it would be a fairly limited operation to retake coastal areas and get back to normal maritime traffic.”
The Houthis have become Iran’s most formidable ally in the Middle East since Israel’s degradation of Hezbollah in Lebanon over the past three years.

A Saudi-directed offensive against the group would mark a new flashpoint in a region engulfed by conflict since the Hamas-led attacks on Israel of Oct. 7, 2023, and the subsequent US-Israeli war on Iran.

Washington, Saudi Arabia’s most powerful ally, is providing military advisers and intelligence, including targeting information, to support Saudi air operations in Yemen, according to one of the Western diplomats.

However, the extent of support may be limited. Reuters has previously reported that US President Donald Trump rebuffed requests by the de facto Saudi ruler Mohammed bin Salman for direct military support such as air strikes.
Turkey and Pakistan, with whom Saudi Arabia signed a joint defense agreement last month, have provided military equipment that the kingdom is using in Yemen, Pakistani and regional officials said.

Last month, Pakistan sent four cargo planes with equipment including air defense systems, light artillery, drones and anti-drone systems to Aden, the seat of Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, a Pakistani government official said.

Pakistani military advisers are also on the ground with Saudi counterparts to support Yemeni forces, according to a second Pakistani official, the Gulf official and a Western diplomat. Turkish drones, bought by Saudi Arabia before the current war, have also been deployed over Yemen, they added.

One of the kingdom’s key concerns in launching a new offensive in Yemen is how to protect its oil facilities and other infrastructure from Houthi drone and missile attacks, according to regional officials who said Riyadh has asked several allies for help with defensive systems.

Pakistan has deployed between 30,000 and 40,000 troops to Saudi Arabia to help defend the kingdom’s land borders and help with drone and missile interceptions, according to the second Pakistani official, who said the troops arrived in waves beginning last year but also after the recent escalation. Islamabad hasn’t made any decision to send troops into Yemen in a fighting capacity, the official said.
The Pakistani and Turkish defense ministries didn’t respond to requests for comment on their military support for Riyadh.
France, meanwhile, has announced it will send defensive systems and troops to Saudi Arabia to help protect the Red Sea port city of Yanbu.

Any ground operation inside Yemen will rely on the disparate coalition of Yemeni fighting factions that Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates armed and trained at earlier stages of the civil war when the conflict ground to a bloody stalemate.

“Many anti-Houthi forces are still not organized or prepared for the kind of sustained offensive required to push back a disciplined Houthi military force. And they are being tested right now, as the Houthis apply pressure across several fronts at once,” said Yemen analyst Mohammed Albasha.

Yemeni forces were further fractured last winter when southern fighters backed by the UAE tried to take territory in the east and announce secession plans, leading to their defeat by Saudi-backed fighters after a series of clashes.
Ali Shihabi, a Saudi political analyst close to government thinking, cautioned that the outcome of any offensive by the Saudis against the Houthis would depend on how ground forces perform.

“The priority so far has been to defend the positions on the ground and stabilize the front, but certainly they will be going on the offensive,” he said. “Success greatly depends on the quality of the performance of the local forces.”

The day before we spoke, King1, 26, had learned that his friend Lamont had been killed. He was at home when his cousin called to break the news and asked him to come over. ‘I’m on my way,’ King replied immediately, knowing what was being asked of him. He ran up to his room to retrieve his Glock, opened his box of bullets and, one by one, filled the clip.

Lamont was dead, though King couldn’t fully wrap his mind around the fact. He’d seen him only hours earlier, when Lamont and King’s cousin stopped by his house. They’d been shot at by their rivals the day before, and King had warned them to be careful: ‘Y’all need to keep y’alls’ heads up.’ Now the car Lamont died in sat empty on a nearby street, shot up and stained with his blood. King watched a video posted on Facebook of paramedics draping the body with a sheet and carrying it into an ambulance.

King knew what came next. He and his cousin would go out with their guns and ride through the neighbourhood until they found the men responsible. ‘I just wanted my get-back,’ he said. He wanted the people who killed Lamont to feel what he was feeling. And if he couldn’t find them, he’d find someone else he had beef with. King reasoned: ‘It could be a person who I don’t like or who I’m already into it with. I’m going to slide on them too and whoever else. That’s how I grew up with my feelings. That’s how I let off my rage.’

To King, retaliation felt less like a choice than an inevitability. ‘Whether I do it or not, somebody going to do it,’ he said. ‘If it ain’t me, I got other homies who feel the same way I feel. I got cousins, family members, they mommas. That’s how it be, and that’s how it’s going to always be. It’s a repeated cycle.’
His clip was full. Then King decided to do something that a year earlier he would not have done.

For King, and for many Americans like him, gun violence is not an exceptional event but a fact of life. In some parts of the United States, lethal violence has reached a scale exceeding recent wars and military occupations. Between 2020 and 2021, a young man in Chicago’s Garfield Park neighbourhood, where King is from, faced a higher risk of being killed than a US soldier deployed to Afghanistan or Iraq. By age 40, around half of the city’s Black and Hispanic residents will have witnessed someone being shot.

Violent crime has fallen steeply across the US since 2021, though not everywhere. According to Chicago’s crime dashboard, fatal shootings in Chicago were up 7 per cent this year as of late September. But even in cities where the decline has held, a citywide figure is a poor description of how violence is experienced. In US cities, most shootings concentrate in a few dozen blocks and among a few hundred people who account for less than 1 per cent of a city’s population. Thus, citywide numbers cannot capture what it is like to live inside that zone, where violence is not a discrete event but an experience that leaves stubborn traces on many lives.

In 2022, I was part of a research team that interviewed 99 men from Chicago’s highest-violence neighbourhoods. All were former or current participants in the Rapid Employment and Development Initiative, or READI Chicago, a community violence intervention run by a partnership of Heartland Alliance, the University of Chicago and seven nonprofit organisations on the city’s south and west sides. READI served adult men at greatest risk of shooting someone or being shot. By the time they entered the programme, 98 per cent had been arrested, averaging more than 17 times each, and 35 per cent had been shot. For 18 months, participants were paid to work and attend group cognitive behavioural intervention (CBI) sessions. Outreach workers helped them navigate housing, legal, safety and substance-use crises that might otherwise have made steady participation difficult.
The men had learned to anticipate danger in ordinary moments and to meet it by fighting back

We asked each person we spoke with to tell us the story of his life, then to reconstruct minor confrontations, conflicts averted, and those that escalated into violence. We asked what they had been thinking and feeling as these events unfolded, returning to a single question: ‘What was going through your mind when that happened?’ Our aim was to access a layer of cognition beneath the behaviour, and to understand how the men made sense of their own actions and those of others.

Our conversations revealed something important about what violence teaches the mind. Lives spent amid violence meant the men had learned to anticipate danger in ordinary moments and to meet it by fighting back. The premise of READI’s work, and our research, is that because this way of seeing was learned, it could also be unlearned.

The danger these men read into the world is real; recall that more than a third of them had been shot. The difficulty is that a mind shaped by real danger does not confine its lessons to dangerous situations. It brings them into ambiguous ones, where the reading is wrong often enough to produce the very danger it anticipates. The outer world and the inner one are not separate. A world of violence sustains itself not only through guns, poverty and other social ills, but also through the ways of seeing it produces. Our research asks where these patterns of seeing and responding come from, why they persist, and how they can change.
Again and again, three patterns surfaced that could make future violence more likely.

The first was misreading situations. A great deal of violence, the men told us, stems from misconstruing some aspect of an interpersonal interaction, such as the nature of the situation or the other person’s intent. Past experiences of violence had created threat-oriented frames that quickly registered ambiguous cues as dangerous. Nuke, 24, told us that even a stranger looking at him for too long could escalate into a confrontation: ‘Sometimes I’ll react. Like: “Man, what the fuck is you looking at?”’

Tim, now 30, traced this reactive impulse to being shot and nearly killed at 17. ‘I was young in the streets, so I was always an impulsive person,’ he recalled. ‘But it got really bad after [I was shot]. I felt like the world was against me … If you approach me a certain type of way and if you wasn’t a person I was with on a daily basis, I felt like you was my enemy.’ Even casual remarks became charged: ‘Before that incident, I’ll be like: “Man, whatever.” But now it’s like: “Man, what you mean by that?… You saying that you going to shoot me?”’ Like many others we spoke with, Tim had lost loved ones to gun violence and had been shot at himself. But a mind tuned to danger could also misread ordinary situations, reproducing the violence that had trained it.

The second pattern was a narrowing of perceived response options. When violence seemed possible, those we spoke with often saw only a narrow set of things they could do. Kobe, 24, described the months after his release from prison: ‘I was walking around like a ticking time bomb. Soon as somebody did anything, I’m whooping them like I’m they daddy.’ Similarly, when King learned that Lamont was dead, his thoughts narrowed to one response: revenge.

Such narrowing can be adaptive in dangerous situations, where hesitation can be costly. But when it is applied more generally, it can lead to serious problems. In these moments, people tend to bypass deliberate reflection and may feel that certain responses are inevitable, as King told us: ‘That’s how it be, and that’s how it’s going to always be. It’s a repeated cycle.’

Third, our interviews revealed that participants often read violent behaviour as proof of who someone was, rather than how that person had responded to a situation. Psychologists call this the fundamental attribution error, or our tendency to explain behaviour through features of a person’s character rather than circumstance. But the men turned this error most mercilessly on themselves.
Accepting violence as part of who they were made their future involvement in violence more likely

Take William, who had lost 11 close friends to gun violence by the age of 29. He came to see revenge not as something he did but as something he was. ‘I ain’t been a civilian since I was like eight…,’ he told us. ‘To sleep at night [with what I’ve done] you got to be a different type of monster.’ After his best friend was killed, he said: ‘I bought guns, a lot of them … I wasn’t going to feel safe until somebody was dead.’ Over time, the identity hardened: ‘To put that bet on somebody else, you got to be a cold-hearted motherfucker. Melatonin can’t even help you sleep after that.’

Terrel, 29, had endured a childhood of compounding losses. His mother was incarcerated, his little sister killed in a house fire, and he was shot – all before finishing the eighth grade. ‘I was an angry-ass little kid,’ he recalled. ‘I was angry because my momma was gone … My little sister dead … Everything I got is gone, so I’m angry.’ Terrel came to read his anger and the violent behaviour it spawned as a verdict on himself. Beneath the easy smile others saw, he felt he was ‘just covering up [what’s inside] with that smile’: ‘I been fucking up the community for years. How the fuck am I good?’

In sum, many we spoke to had come to see themselves not simply as people who had done bad things, but as bad people. By their own accounts, accepting violence as part of who they were made their future involvement in violence more likely.

Violence alters how people experience the world and read everyday encounters. These patterns are neither irrational nor pathological. They are adaptations to real danger, where quick responses can save a life. But carried into the wrong situation, the same shortcuts can be overgeneralised in ways that cause grave harm.

While the stakes of these cognitive patterns are exceptional, the mental machinery underpinning them is not. Say you’re driving and another car cuts you off. Before you’ve even thought about it, your mind has supplied a reason: This driver is reckless and has no regard for anyone else on the road. The interpretation arrives in a split second, built more out of your irritation than anything you know about the driver. Maybe she’s racing to a hospital for an emergency. The writer David Foster Wallace described such a scene in his commencement speech, ‘This Is Water’ (2005). His point was hopeful: we are free to choose how we read such a moment. The automatic, egocentric perspective is never the only one available.

Nuke’s mind did the same when a stranger held his gaze too long. The look may have meant nothing, yet he imagined a motive and a threat, drawn from his life, as most of us do, rather than anything the stranger had done. Nuke is working with the same machinery as the rest of us. What that machinery was trained on is different, and so is the price of getting it wrong. For the driver, a misreading ends in a muttered curse or a blown horn; for Nuke, it could end a life. As Nuke admitted: ‘I know what comes with it. It’s either death or jail.’

We tend to imagine that we take in the world and then respond to what we find. In fact, the mind guides what we see, filling gaps with expectations built from experience. The journalist Walter Lippmann in 1922 called these expectations ‘the pictures in our heads’ and explained that it is the pictures we respond to, not some objective environmental stimuli. Psychologists and sociologists call these shortcuts frames and scripts. Frames answer, in a fraction of a second, the question under every social encounter: What is going on here? Scripts suggest what to do next. Together they help us move through our days without deliberating over each interaction. Frames and scripts are tools that make daily life possible.
The vigilance that keeps someone alive at one point can generate danger at another

Among the men we spoke with, these shortcuts took their shape from a world that taught a brutal lesson early: people are dangerous, and hesitation can get you hurt. The lesson came from somewhere. The sociologist Elijah Anderson in 1994 called it the ‘code of the streets’. Where safety is not a given, a reputation for violence becomes the protection people can supply themselves. The frame comes first: this is a threat. The script that follows, I have to fight back, is learned from experience and reinforced by others.

But a shortcut is only as good as it is accurate. Threat-oriented frames and scripts may be adaptive in the specific situations that produced them, but the same reading carried into an uncertain moment can be destructive and self-defeating. The vigilance that keeps someone alive at one point can generate danger at another, converting an ambiguous situation into a hostile one and producing the very conflict it anticipated. The mind continues to guard against a world that is, in part, no longer there.

Of course, the milieu that trained these frames and scripts has not entirely disappeared for most. Recall that young men in these neighbourhoods faced a greater risk of being killed than a soldier deployed to Iraq or Afghanistan. A soldier, though, eventually returns home; these men have no such separation. What they must learn is more complex: how to hold on to vigilance without letting it dictate their reactions in the wrong place or at the wrong moment. The problem is not the impulse to fight back itself, but being unable to distinguish situations that call for it from those that don’t.

The idea that changing how we see can change how we respond is ancient. In the 2nd century, Epictetus said: ‘Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of them.’ What is unusual is its application. Offering the opportunity to reframe a situation, as a serious answer to lethal violence, to a 26-year-old sitting in his room with a loaded clip is a novel proposition. It begins from an assumption too rarely extended to men like King with a history of violence: that despite what he has been through, his inner life is not fixed.

READI offered men a chance to discipline their inner worlds. The 18-month intervention paired a part-time job with cognitive behavioural sessions, held three to five mornings a week, that participants called ‘CAD’ (Control-Alt-Delete, the keystroke that reboots a computer). The lessons taught participants how to slow down to reconsider an automatic reaction and widen the range of responses in a tense moment. They learned that they did not have to be ruled by their first feeling or thought. In doing so, they began to loosen the identity that violence had formed

A randomised controlled trial of READI estimated that participants were arrested for shootings and homicides 65 per cent less often than comparable men who were not offered the programme. Findings from a related programme point in the same direction. Becoming a Man, a school-based programme run in Chicago by the nonprofit organisation Youth Guidance, cut violent-crime arrests among high-school-age participants by nearly half. Our interviews complement these trials by showing what the changes these programmes brought felt like from the inside.
What seemed to be a threat from the man across the street might be coming from somewhere much older

The first thing the men learned was to question their reading of a situation. In one CAD session, the group was given a scenario: somebody walks past and calls you a name. What do you do? For TY, 20, who had spent his adolescence surviving, the old answer would have arrived without thought. Instead, he worked through it. ‘I ain’t got no right to cause hurt to another person [if] this person ain’t do nothing to me,’ he said. ‘He probably having a bad day. He probably just got into it with his wife. You don’t know what’s wrong.’ Such exercises helped participants practise reframing a situation more charitably.

Questioning a reading also meant learning that a feeling of threat was not always about what was happening in the present; sometimes, it was a reaction to events in the past. The men practised noticing what fear was doing in their bodies, such as a racing pulse, tightened fists, pressure in the chest, and learning to treat those sensations as signals to investigate rather than signs of objective threats. Larry, 31, described it as learning to check in with his body: ‘Far as articulating the things that’s going on inside of my body and how I’m feeling, that’s what I’m really learning.’ What seemed to be a threat from the man across the street might, at times, be coming from somewhere much older.

Second, they learned to see more than one possible response to feeling threatened. Kobe described his old reflex as follows: ‘If you said something, I was going to touch you or tap you or get on your ass.’ Now, Kobe said: ‘I think before I act.’ Recalling a role-play in which he was bumped outside a store, he laid out what he could now see: ‘I could whoop one of they ass and one of them could shoot me… or I could just walk away. Or I could ask him, did he mean to do it?’ Three options emerged where there had previously been one.

To help them remember they had options in the moment, the men developed mantras simple enough to recall under pressure. Keith, 24, learned to: ‘Take 10 deep breaths, pace back and forth, and you might see things differently.’ Tune, 30, used: ‘It only takes three seconds to ruin your life.’ Larry, in a fight with his son’s mother, told himself: ‘It’s just words.’

Finally, participants learned to distinguish what they had done from who they were. Jaysean, 22, had taken the bad things he had done as proof that he was a bad person. Abandoned by kin while still a boy, he had sought out older robbers to teach him how to survive. He said: ‘A lot of things that I did bad, I did it for survival. Cause I didn’t really know no other way to get no money.’ Jaysean explained: ‘I was looking for the wrong help. I didn’t know no better. You a product of your environment to a certain extent.’ The reframing allowed him to imagine a self no longer defined by his past: ‘I’m a good person within… I’m still falling down but I’m picking myself back up.’ What Jaysean had once believed was a sign of his character, he could now see as a result of surviving tough circumstances.

Terrel reached the same realisation by naming the trauma he had long carried. ‘I never got through my first trauma,’ he said of his sister’s death; in the years since, he had lost a brother, a cousin, a nephew and friend after friend. ‘That shit just fucked me up to this day. I’m suffering with PTSD bad.’ Understanding his behaviour as a response to those losses, rather than as proof of who he was, made change imaginable. As Terrel said: ‘If you don’t deal with it… you can bring that baggage into your adult life.’ Naming the ways in which his past spilled into the present through his PTSD allowed Terrel to challenge his own narrative about himself and begin to heal.

These are ancient skills. READI’s contribution was not inventing them but building a place where men could practise them. These changes required certain conditions. READI’s wages gave the men enough stability to keep returning, and staff created a space safe enough for them to lower their guard, even around those participants they previously considered rivals. The pay check may have been what initially brought them in, but it was not how they ultimately understood the programme. In fact, 70 per cent described READI primarily as an opportunity for personal growth rather than just a job, and they spoke at length about how it reshaped their closest relationships, their daily habits, even their sense of who they were.

Which brings us back to King, in his room, with the clip full. Despite his initial instincts, he did not join his cousin to retaliate. He put the gun down and stayed put. ‘So I got high and I sat right there and just calmed myself down,’ he told us. ‘I shed a couple of tears for my boy and said: “Everything going to be all right.”’ It was the very mantra he had been practising in READI. King’s grief had not abated. What had changed was that revenge no longer felt inevitable. ‘Why I go try to waste my life for nothing?’ he asked. ‘That’s not me no more.’ In the space between feeling and action, King could see another response.

King did not arrive at that response alone. For months, he had practised slowing down and questioning his first reaction with other men. READI did not make the danger around him less real, nor did it ask him to abandon the vigilance that had sometimes kept him alive. Rather, it helped him more clearly discern the moments it threatened to reproduce the very violence he feared.

This is where I part with Wallace. He was right that we can choose how to read a situation, but he underestimated what such a choice requires. For the men we interviewed, seeing differently was not just a private act of will performed alone in traffic. It was something they practised repeatedly with others, under conditions of safety, enough time and skilled support.
‘I didn’t know that if you yelled at me, I was gonna break down. But now I [see]: it’s not you, it’s a past trigger’

I have seen the same skills taught in a classroom, on a corner by an outreach worker, and in a boxing gym in the Chicago neighbourhood of North Lawndale, where the former gang member Derek Brown* has been running a programme called Boxing Out Negativity since 2009. He teaches boys to box and, alongside it, to sit still and breathe, to notice what their bodies are doing before a fight and after one, to name what they are feeling and to wait. The boys come to Derek’s gym to learn how to fight. They are also learning how to handle the moments before a fight starts, which is the harder lesson and the one they need more often in life.

These skills are also useful to people who meet others in moments of crises. LaToya Baines* manages victim advocates on Chicago’s West Side who spend their days supporting people through the worst moments of their lives, and who bring their own histories to that work. She learned the same techniques through training and now teaches them to her staff. ‘Once you learn, you’re able to identify those triggers. I didn’t know that if you yelled at me, I was gonna break down. But now I’m able to [see]: it’s not you, it’s a past trigger. I just stepped back into the past, for something else that happened to me that has nothing to do with you.’ Chicago police officers are being taught to do the same thing, through a programme called Situational Decision-Making. Officers who went through it used less force and made fewer discretionary arrests.

None of this is particular to places where violence is the problem. When my husband and I started having conversations about merging our finances, I would respond by shutting down and becoming frustrated. He studies financial decision-making for a living, and talking about money was second-nature to him. For me it was physically painful. My chest would tighten, and I would go quiet, get anxious or find a reason to end the conversation.

It took me a long time to understand why. In the family in which I grew up, we didn’t talk about money. When we had it, nobody mentioned it. Then we lost our house, my parents divorced, and money was a more frequently discussed issue. It wasn’t until years later, while having conversations about finances with my husband that stirred negative responses in me, that I recognised how I automatically logged a conversation about money as the beginning of something going wrong. With help from a cognitive behavioural therapist and my very patient husband, I learned what the men in READI learned: to notice a reactive feeling in my body, to have compassion for myself about where it came from, and to recognise when it no longer served me.

Violence teaches the mind what to expect and how to answer. Because these are learned habits, they can be remade. A mind formed amid violence is not fixed by it. But few people revise their habits of mind on their own, sitting in traffic and deciding to see things differently. With proper training, people can learn to question their first reading of a situation, to see more than one response available to them, and to stop taking what they have done as proof of who they are. They learn, in other words, that their pasts need not define their present. The capacity is ordinary. What is not is the safety and ongoing support it takes to use it.

Ella Langley’s hot streak isn’t slowing down, but that doesn’t mean her Dandelion tour will last forever. The tour runs through the end of this month, with dates in Colorado at the iconic Red Rocks Amphitheatre, L.A., and yes, Texas; she’ll perform at Lubbock’s United Supermarkets Arena on Oct. 10.

Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” officially overtook Mariah Carey’s “All I Want For Christmas Is You” as the longest-running Number One song in Billboard Hot 100 history. And while a common sentiment on social media is to claim ignorance of the hit track, fans are clearly turning out for Langley, whose concert dates have sold out across the country.
